short: A non-aggression treaty between sworn enemies that opened the way into Poland.
full:
On 23 August 1939 Joachim von Ribbentrop flew to Moscow and signed a non-aggression treaty with Vyacheslav Molotov, with Stalin standing behind them. That two regimes built on mutual hatred should come to terms astonished the world. German and Soviet negotiators had in fact been trading proposals for weeks, while Britain and France conducted unhurried military talks in Moscow through a delegation sent by slow steamer.

The published text promised neutrality. A secret protocol divided eastern Europe: Finland, Estonia, Latvia and eastern Poland to the Soviet sphere, Lithuania and western Poland to Germany, with Lithuania traded across in a later amendment. Freed from the risk of a war on two fronts, Germany invaded Poland on 1 September and Soviet forces crossed the eastern frontier on the 17th. The Soviet Union went on to annex the Baltic states and attack Finland, and shipped Germany grain and oil until the morning Hitler broke the pact in June 1941. Moscow denied the protocol existed until 1989.
